items.title: @shostekofsky There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a ...
items.content:
@shostekofsky There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

items.title: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a va...
items.content:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

items.title:
Kimi-K3.1-Pro by Moonshot AI: interesting facts

It's huge, and sparse
• It has 2.8T total parameter...
items.content:
Kimi-K3.1-Pro by Moonshot AI: interesting facts

It's huge, and sparse
• It has 2.8T total parameters, but only 104B are active per token.
• Along with Kimi-K3, it's the largest real model release on the Hub. The next biggest are Qwen3.8-2.4T and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T).
• It has 896 experts and sends each token to 16 of them. (DeepSeek-V4-Pro has 2 times less and Mistral-Large-4 has 7 times less)

Clever attention for a 1M-token context
• Most of its 93 layers use linear attention (KDA). Every 4th layer uses DeepSeek-style sparse attention, which only looks at the top 2048 tokens.
• This is how it handles a 1M-token context (the same as the other frontier open models)
• It uses a custom activation called SiTU-GLU and has a 401M-parameter vision encoder (MoonViT-V2), so it takes both text and images.

Small on disk for its size
• It was trained to run in 4-bit (MXFP4), so the whole repo is only ~1.56 TB.
• Stored in regular BF16 it would be about 5.6 TB(!)
 
Benchmarks (from the model card)
• It goes back and forth with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. It's top of the card's table on BrowseComp (92.1), HLE with tools (70.0) and SWE Marathon (51.7).
• It's weaker on pure reasoning without tools and on cyber security.
• Moonshot ran most of their own coding evals using the Claude Code harness.

License (a modified MIT)
• It's free to use, modify and redistribute.
• API businesses making over $20M a year need a deal with Moonshot.
• Products with over 100M monthly users or over $20M monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3.1-Pro".

On the Hub
• It went public about 1.5 hours ago and already has 214 likes, about 9× Kimi-K3's first hour. It's #19 on the trending list.
• It isn't gated, but loading it in transformers requires "trust_remote_code"

items.title: Announcing the next version of Artificial Analysis API Performance Benchmarking: Time per Task is no...
items.content:
Announcing the next version of Artificial Analysis API Performance Benchmarking: Time per Task is now our headline performance metric, measuring how long a model takes to complete a task rather than how fast it streams

The update applies to the ~1,000 serverless endpoints we benchmark multiple times a day for speed, latency and caching.

Key changes:
➤ Time per Task is now the headline metric to compare models: as workloads become more agentic, the time to complete a task matters more than speed per token. A model that is fast per token but verbose can take longer than a slower model that uses fewer tokens. Time per Task divides a model's output tokens per Intelligence Index task by its End-to-End Output Speed.

➤ End-to-End Output Speed covers the full request: speed is now measured from sending the request to receiving the final token. That includes the wait before the first token (prefill, and reasoning for models that hide it) as well as generation. Output tokens now come from each provider's API-reported counts instead of the o200k_base tokenizer, and we monitor for discrepancies in reported counts.

➤ Agentic workloads are now part of every measurement: we benchmark short, document-length and long-context prompts, plus multi-turn sessions across coding and knowledge work. Headline figures are the average across these workloads over the past 5 days.

➤ API default effort is now tracked alongside highest effort: most developers run models at the effort level each lab sets as its API default, so we now benchmark key models at that setting as well as at their highest effort. Effort names are not comparable across labs, so we use each lab's own default rather than one shared setting.

Key takeaways:
➤ OpenAI models make up most of the Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier despite slower output speeds: across effort levels, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol hold the frontier from ~45 to ~55 on the Intelligence Index. At max effort, GPT-6 Astra runs at 51 tokens/s but finishes a task in ~17 minutes, against ~26 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 111 tokens/s) and ~29 minutes for Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 71 tokens/s), because it uses ~50k output tokens per task against ~120k to ~170k.

➤ API default effort cuts Time per Task by ~3 to 5x and Cost per Task by ~2 to 4x for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5: all three default to medium effort, which scores ~5 to 11 points lower on the Intelligence Index in exchange. Claude Opus 5.5 falls from ~26 minutes and $10.04 per task at max to ~6.8 minutes and $2.45 at medium effort.

➤ Endpoints that optimize for decode speed alone see the largest drop in End-to-End Output Speed: high decode speeds can come at the cost of latency, for example by queuing requests to run at lower batch sizes, or by holding output and sending it in a single burst. Both lengthen the wait before the first token, which End-to-End Output Speed now counts.

items.title:
There is a false equivalence being made between open source software and AI benchmarks.  

The argum...
items.content:
There is a false equivalence being made between open source software and AI benchmarks.  

The argument is that  we shouldn't expend effort criticizing benchmarks, and should instead improve them. 

Unlike OSS software, benchmark results are consumed for decision making at face value.  They are currently used like Yelp or a credit score, and less like a informative dataset you can analyze

Benchmarks don't come with disclaimers, and people don't realize how brittle they can be.  Consumers don't have the data skills to analyze the traces and see the limitations of benchmarks.  Hell people who have the skills don't question it either, and are SHOCKED when they see the traces. 

So yeah, I think more people should have healthy skepticism.  Right now, most people don't realize what they are looking at.  The biggest problem is the large dissonance between the marketing of benchmarks and what they really measure.  

Instead of deflecting the criticisms of benchmarks, I think the communications need to be fixed around them.

He calls for healthy skepticism and better communication rather than deflecting criticism.

Dessa lead @RagavanThura...
items.content:
Block trained its new voice AI entirely on speech, without using any text.

Dessa lead @RagavanThurair says even his team didn't expect it to develop such strong language understanding:

"It's trained entirely on speech, which is crazy. This company's training it just on speech, they have less data, it's a lot harder, how the hell are they gonna learn language like that? But somehow ours ended up better."

"I thought we would have to have text to get to this level of conversation understanding. We didn't expect it would learn language this good."

"People have done this before, like GSLM and Hertz-dev. The big gap is ours has a really strong understanding of language and you can actually have a realistic conversation with it."
@blocks

items.content:
I managed to port Battlefield 1942 to mobile web too

So now it's playable as full multiplayer on iPhone and Android from their browser! 🤯

Claude Code built its own graphic layer that translates Direct3D (DirectX) instructions to WebGL, sitting between the game's machine code and the browser, which means we can change the resolution any way we want!

Only issue is you get some stuff cutting off (like the arms below or inside vehicles) because the game was never meant to run in portrait mode of course!

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI is buying Pierre, a startup that set out to build a better GitHub, to power Codex.

• Pierre makes Code Storage, Git hosting built for software that writes code, plus the open-source libraries Trees and Diffs
• Trees and Diffs already run file browsing and code review inside the Codex app
• Code Storage's features will move into Codex, and Pierre's open-source projects will stay open
• OpenAI has also built Pando, an internal source control system for agents working in parallel, which reportedly cut deployment latency by about 80%
• Pierre had about 10 employees, and OpenAI didn't disclose the price
• Jacob Thornton co-created Bootstrap at Twitter in 2011

@sophiadew: "The original pitch that Pierre had for what it was supposed to be was building a better GitHub."

items.title: Democrats just won both chambers of Congress. But sweeping AI safety legislation is far from guarant...
items.content:
Democrats just won both chambers of Congress. But sweeping AI safety legislation is far from guaranteed.

@NathanLeamerDC explains why cybersecurity could be the real bipartisan path to AI regulation:

"A Democrat House and Senate are still gonna be at odds with the White House."

"There's still Democrats who are not fully on board with the more safetyist doomer crowd, and on the right there’s a freedom caucus of AI safetyists, but a small minority."

"Anthropic came out with their proposal, it even had preemption of the states, something they were opposing for years, and then they were attacked by activists left of center and switched their position over a weekend."

"I'm not so sure we're gonna see a big beautiful bill for AI. The larger question is, is there a cybersecurity measure that could be passed?"

"When you talk about AI safety in relation to cybersecurity, you bring a lot more people to the table. When you talk about catastrophic risk, it turns a lot of people off on both sides."

items.summary: MTSlive reports that despite Democrats winning both chambers of Congress, comprehensive AI safety legislation remains unlikely, quoting policy analyst Nathan Leamer on divided government, splits within both parties over AI safety, Anthropic's reversal on a preemption-containing proposal after activist pushback, and cybersecurity as the most plausible bipartisan regulatory path.

items.title: Most leading labs set their API default below their highest effort, which cuts Time per Task sharply...
items.content: Most leading labs set their API default below their highest effort, which cuts Time per Task sharply. At medium effort, GPT-6 Astra scores 52 on the Intelligence Index against 57 at max, but finishes a task in ~5.8 minutes instead of ~18. GPT-6.1 Sol drops from 55 to 46 at 3.9 minutes instead of 20.0, and Claude Opus 5.5 from 59 to 48 at 6.8 minutes instead of 26.0.

All are established models per GA dates, so this is measurement analysis rather than launch news.

items.title: Block's @RagavanThurair tested AI voice models by making sounds of pain. They thought he was stretch...
items.content:
Block's @RagavanThurair tested AI voice models by making sounds of pain. They thought he was stretching or waking up.

He warns that this could become a serious safety problem as AI-powered robots gain more autonomy:

"I tried to make sounds of pain. I had this experience recently where my toddler stepped on a sensitive part of my body, and I couldn't say words. All I could do is make sounds of pain. Imagine a Unitree robot steps on me the same way. I can’t say words to say, get off of me."

"These models fail at that. It's like, oh, it sounds like you're stretching. Did you just wake up? It doesn't understand crying and things like that. There's a reason why we can hear emotion in voice."

"I think it's actually a huge safety issue as well. These AI models are taking more and more control of things."

"They're extremely smart, but if they don’t understand what we actually want or what we're trying to communicate, they can end up doing things we don't want."
@blocks

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: SpaceX just opened Starfall, its capsule for making drugs and materials in spac...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: SpaceX just opened Starfall, its capsule for making drugs and materials in space, to commercial customers.

• Each mission can be tailored for weeks of continuous microgravity before the capsule reenters and splashes down off California
• SpaceX's FAA filings call it "a mass producible reentry vehicle" meant to help "create a self-sustaining commercial in-space manufacturing market"
• It flew demo missions in June and October, and SpaceX signed 3 commercial missions in the third quarter
• European firms Exolaunch and Space Cargo Unlimited booked Starfall flights on Starship in September
• Merck has grown Keytruda crystals on the ISS since 2014, and that research helped lead to the 1-minute injection the FDA approved in September 2025

@sophiadew: "If you think about innovation and just how humans have evolved, a lot of it has been around our ability to transform materials into everyday substances, maybe we'll have different types of crystals or maybe types of semiconductors and optical fibers."

@sarahcat21 I think that there are two different things going on re: BenchGate

1. There are some ha...
items.content:
@sarahcat21 I think that there are two different things going on re: BenchGate

1. There are some hardworking people making the benchmarks with the best intentions.

2. People are consuming the benchmark blindly, putting too much weight on it.
Other people, with something to gain from the benchmark repackage or promote them etc., giving those benchmarks more authority then is warranted. 

BenchMark gate mostly about the second group, I think. BUT the first group should be more aware of the second group, in some cases it is willful complicity but we can assume best intentions 

This is why it’s very different than OSS and “everyone benefits from the commons” and is more nuanced

items.content:
This model helps robots learn to manipulate objects physically.

But there's something really interesting about it:

The model learns skills from humans rather than relying on robot demonstrations, which are much more expensive and time-consuming.

Basically, this model lets robots perform zero-shot tasks without training on robot demonstrations collected specifically for those tasks.

They demonstrated this:

• 60 tasks and 600 trials
• 63.5% success on pick-and-place tasks
• 34.0% success on other manipulation tasks
• 10.5% success on challenging/long-horizon tasks

items.content:
@sarahcat21 It’s sometimes both, seems more probable to include benchmark creators when they profit from the benchmark (selling the data, services etc) 

It’s always good to assume best intentions. I’m not interested in blaming anyone.  Right now there is a massive misunderstanding of what these numbers actually mean.

I think everybody needs to work together, benchmark creators included to help bridge the gap in the public’s understanding.

Benchmarks will always be flawed no matter what, so I think the comms are what’s important and missing here.  

Also, I don’t think people pointing out the flaws are coming from a place of vitriol towards benchmark creators. I think they’re motivated by trying to address this misunderstanding, and are largely outspoken among the sea of “this one number is all you need” thrown at them by the industrial-benchmark complex.

"How do you interrogate algorithms?"

Former DOJ antitrust chief @dohamekki explains how AI agents are creating an entirely new challenge for law enforcement:

"Small groups of people are going to be the ones who are first in the door thinking about how to enforce laws that the American people desperately need enforced. I would have brought many more cases if I had had FluxCap."

"There are products being shipped that the general counsel of companies don’t even fully understand."

"That's a tough environment for companies that do not understand their technology."

"When prosecutors subpoena information, you're often dealing with human sources. We're in an environment now where agents have logs."

"The question is going to be, how do you interrogate algorithms? That's a sea change."
@fluxcapHQ

Former DOJ antitrust leaders @JKBustertruster and @dohamekki teamed up with ex-Palantir engineers to build an AI litigation platform.

Kanter: "We took a bunch of our former colleagues from the Department of Justice and a team of former Palantir engineers, and we worked together in a fully integrated way from the outset."

"You wouldn’t hire a tax lawyer to litigate an antitrust case. That domain expertise is going to require deep legal technology. It’s out in the wild. People are using it already."

Kanter: "We started with antitrust, and we're already onto our second practice area, which I can't disclose today, but should be rolling out in the coming months."

How to turn your tasks into workflows and reusable behavior.

You ask your agent to build it once, a...
items.content:
How to turn your tasks into workflows and reusable behavior.

You ask your agent to build it once, and then you run it again and again.

Huge advantage to doing this:

• You only use models for tasks that only models can do
• Every other step is encoded in TypeScript
• Very easy to troubleshoot

items.title: Modern multimodal AI systems struggle significantly when interpreting structured images such as char...
items.content:
Modern multimodal AI systems struggle significantly when interpreting structured images such as charts, data plots, and geometric diagrams. Unlike natural photographs, these graphics require exact symbolic interpretation; a minor perceptual slip, such as slightly misreading an axis tick or a data bar, can trigger cascading reasoning failures. Previous attempts to improve accuracy have relied either on purely textual step-by-step reasoning or on rigid, one-way image edits. These conventional methods suffer from low visual fidelity and linear workflows that force models into an inflexible monologue, preventing them from revisiting earlier assumptions or exploring alternate visual interpretations.

The article introduces and evaluates PixelCraft, a specialized multi-agent framework designed to deliver high-fidelity image editing and flexible, non-linear reasoning across structured visuals. The core objective is to demonstrate that combining specialized image-grounding tools with dynamic, multi-agent collaboration significantly improves the accuracy and reliability of leading vision-language models on complex analytical tasks.

items.content:
Modern generative AI can now produce highly photorealistic imagery, yet these outputs frequently harbor subtle semantic errors such as impossible physics, biological flaws, or contradictory object interactions. While traditional digital forensics focuses on imperceptible pixel textures or lighting artifacts, it fails to explain high-level commonsense violations that human observers notice and distrust. Addressing this gap is critical for establishing visual media authenticity, auditing generative models, and providing interpretable forensics in high-stakes domains.

The article introduces and formalizes the task of semantic visual anomaly detection and reasoning for synthetic images. Its primary objective is to evaluate how effectively multimodal models can identify content-level errors, articulate why they violate real-world logic, and quantify their severity through structured explanations rather than basic real-or-fake classifications.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/VWfP3GyClm

items.content_html:
Modern generative AI can now produce highly photorealistic imagery, yet these outputs frequently harbor subtle semantic errors such as impossible physics, biological flaws, or contradictory object interactions. While traditional digital forensics focuses on imperceptible pixel textures or lighting artifacts, it fails to explain high-level commonsense violations that human observers notice and distrust. Addressing this gap is critical for establishing visual media authenticity, auditing generative models, and providing interpretable forensics in high-stakes domains.

The article introduces and formalizes the task of semantic visual anomaly detection and reasoning for synthetic images. Its primary objective is to evaluate how effectively multimodal models can identify content-level errors, articulate why they violate real-world logic, and quantify their severity through structured explanations rather than basic real-or-fake classifications.

items.title:
I've spent 3 weeks connecting 40+ workflows and turning them into agents.

This company spent years ...
items.content:
I've spent 3 weeks connecting 40+ workflows and turning them into agents.

This company spent years automating everything they could. They have a buttload of workflows to do different things.

If you know the steps, automating a process is pretty simple. You can build a script that runs on an input and does whatever you want.

But agentic systems are so much more than that!

You don't have to orchestrate every step of a process. You don't have to plan every possible path. Instead, you give the agent a goal and access to the tools it needs.

That's it!

To this day, n8n remains one of the simplest ways to build automations, and they have now introduced Agents as well.

Basically, you can take any workflow you have and give it to the agent as a tool. The agent can now decide which workflow to run and when, based on the ask.

For example, imagine you have three workflows:

1. Retrieve customer information
2. Retrieve a customer support history
3. Email customer

The agent can pull a customer's information, check their support history, and put together an email that addresses their problems.

Before, people made decisions at every step and ran individual workflows.

Now, an agent can stitch workflows together and decide when and how to run them, but each workflow still runs the way you built it.

You get the best of both worlds: the flexibility of agents with the predictability of workflows.

Here is a link to read more about the new n8n Agents: https://t.co/nHESkwlRD6

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
Politics.

Been reading all the news and listening to people talk on audio spaces on both sides.

It's the economy, stupid. 

That's what I take away from last night. Gas prices are hurting everyone, and they spoke clearly last night that we are going in the wrong direction, mostly a repudiation of Trump's wars, which got us the higher gas prices and a far worse position for America with its dealings with Iran, and China.

And a smattering of other things (ICE's brutality, and the ongoing poorly thought though wars, which raised gas prices, amongst other consequences, and lack of leadership in robotics and AI).

How can we all work together to build a better economy?

If the Democrats can lead with their new power and get a better economy, they will do well at next election cycle. 

If not, there will be another swing. 

Do we get a better economy with fewer datacenters? With fewer robots? With less AI? With fewer robotaxis? With fewer rockets and satellites? Fewer innovative autos? 

Will that help us make products and services that make us more relevant to the rest of the world?

So many unanswered questions.

I hope we see @elonmusk (and Trump) move toward the Democrats, and work with them to build a better economy. Trump might not have the intellectual ability to do so, but Elon does. 

And I hope everyone turns down the volume knob on our divisions and work across the aisles to put us in a better situation world wide.

That said, I'm a realist. Lots of people on the left are angry at Elon for bringing us Trump. So I expect Elon to get called in front of congress and given a ton of a hard time for a while. 

But if that's all we do for the next two years politically then it is a lost opportunity to lead us into the future and build our economy to be healthy.

Me? 

I'm going to visit another robot company in Silicon Valley today, and am going to focus my meager efforts on startups, like the farming robot companies at @reservoirfarms, that can help our economy improve and make our kids' lives better. 

What about you?

The Little Go Book by Karl Seguin (2014) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open books.

Go (often referred to as Golang) is an open-source, statically typed, compiled programming language developed by Google. It was created in 2007 by computer science pioneers Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson to address infrastructure complexity, slow compilation, and the challenges of building massive, scalable software systems.

The language is widely celebrated for combining the raw performance and security of a compiled language (like C++) with the simplicity of a dynamic language (like Python).

The original text of the book was published in 2014. ChapterPal has prepared an updated 2026 version with current code snippets and all issues discovered after the original edition was published fixed.

Read the book online on ChapterPal: https://t.co/d4FdDIrzy8

items.content:
The Ultimate Guide to Elixir for Object-Oriented Programmers by Bruce Park is now in @ChapterPal's collection of books openly published online, thanks to the permission of its generous authors.

Elixir is a general-purpose, functional programming language designed for building scalable, highly concurrent, and fault-tolerant applications. Created by José Valim in 2012, it is built on top of the BEAM virtual machine—the same robust engine that powers the Erlang programming language.

Elixir successfully bridges the gap between Erlang's legendary, battle-tested backend architecture and a highly productive, developer-friendly syntax heavily inspired by Ruby.

ChapterPal has two versions of the book to choose from: the author's original version (2017) and an updated version from ChapterPal (2026).

items.title: Trump won in 2024 promising to bring down prices. Two years later, Republicans have lost both chambe...
items.content:
Trump won in 2024 promising to bring down prices. Two years later, Republicans have lost both chambers of Congress.

Economist @Noahpinion argues the Iran war and failure to address inflation were central to the backlash:

"In a democracy, you cannot screw up that bad and not be punished in some way."

"The midterm waves are not always consistent with real policy screw-ups. We had a midterm wave in 2018 before Trump had done anything of policy note other than a tax cut, and in 2010 when Obama had done nothing except policies that people later came to like."

"You can't do something as screw-upy as the Iran war without getting punished. You can't just flagrantly not address the thing you were elected to address and say, screw you on inflation."

"Your kid only has to have one doll instead of seven. Trump just laughed in people’s face about the very issue that was clearly number one in 2024."
